basis_legend.measured: from NOAA/NWS publications or instrument data
basis_legend.expert: published guidance by named coaches/sailmakers/meteorologists (Dellenbaugh, Walker, Adams/Bedford, Gladstone, Nixon, Pline, Legler)
basis_legend.lore: local rule of thumb or single-race anecdote; useful but unverified

caveats: Tactical rules are heuristics; the coach should always weigh them against live wind/current observations.

Exact NOAA current-prediction maxima for Bay Bridge / Thomas Point stations could not be pulled (NOAA API blocked from research environment); app should query NOAA CO-OPS current predictions live rather than rely on the constants here.
Wave/chop descriptions for the Bay are qualitative; no Chesapeake-specific wind-wave table was retrieved.

oscillating.detect: Before the start, sail long on each tack and log high/low headings; average them to get a median. Wind swinging back and forth around the median (unstable post-frontal NW/W air, puffy land-crossing breeze) = oscillating. Without a compass, watch whether windward boats start pointing at your stern (you are headed).
oscillating.play: Tack on headers, stay on the lifted tack, keep off the laylines and near the middle, cross boats when a shift lets you, and within one oscillation period of the mark treat the shift as persistent (sail through headers until you can lay it).
oscillating.say: That's a header past the median — tack now and sail the lift back toward the middle.

persistent.detect: Successive readings trend steadily one way with no return to the old median; forecast front passage, sea-breeze fill or a known clocking trend.
persistent.play: Sail toward the new wind: keep going into the header rather than tacking on it, ignore boats crossing ahead (taking sterns is fine), and do not hit the layline early because the shift will make you overstand.
persistent.say: This shift is persistent, not oscillating — keep sailing into the header; the boats crossing you now will pay later.

geographic.detect: Wind bends near shorelines, river mouths and points. Annapolis examples: NW breeze funnels down the Severn with big left puffs; extra breeze off the Severn and nearest weather shore in westerlies; left shifts filtering down Spa Creek; hot random puffs off Eastport in SW; Annapolis Neck shadows SW breeze.
geographic.play: Treat a predictable geographic bend as a persistent shift for that part of the course: position to be on the inside of the bend when you get there. Convergence (shore on your left looking upwind) gives more pressure; divergence (shore on your right) gives less.
geographic.say: The breeze bends off the Severn here — set up to the left so that Spa Creek lift arrives when you need it.

seaBreeze.detect: Sunny warm day, land warmer than water, weak gradient; morning calm; cumulus building along/over shore first; offshore haze clearing. On the Chesapeake, a SE background veering SW brings it in earlier; a W or NW background gives little or no sea breeze. In spring, cold water vs. warm air can suppress it and give light air overall.
seaBreeze.timing: Fills late morning to early afternoon on suitable days; after establishing, northern-hemisphere sea breezes veer roughly 10 deg/hour (Adams/Bedford, northern US). Annapolis sea breeze is weak and can fight a dying northerly, producing a shifting half-mile neutral zone. Fills more often at Sandy Point (western shore) than Kent Island, creating cross-bay shifts.
seaBreeze.play: Before it fills, left shifts often pay (Annapolis lore). Once established and veering, favor the right; get to the side where it arrives first and be patient in the transition — corners can beat the middle when old and new winds fight.
seaBreeze.say: Cumulus on the western shore and the SE gradient say sea breeze is coming — protect the side it fills from first and expect it to veer right.

clocking_forecast.play: If the forecast shows the wind veering (clockwise) through the race, favor the right side; if backing, favor the left. Before a cold front the wind backs SW->W->NW, then tends to shift right as it arrives; post-frontal NW clocks NE and fades over a few days. Near the mark, never bank on a big forecast shift arriving in time — protect against overstanding.
clocking_forecast.say: Forecast has it veering 20 degrees by mid-race, so I want us right of the fleet on this beat.

deadBreeze_newWind.play: When an old breeze dies and a new direction fills (classic Annapolis easterly after a dying northerly), the far right often pays for the new direction and the far left for the old pressure; the middle usually suffers.
deadBreeze_newWind.say: Old breeze dying, new one coming from the right — commit to a side; the middle is where you park.

starts.rule: Find the favored end by head-to-wind / line bearing
starts.detail: Go head to wind near mid-line (slightly to leeward, or windward in a crowd), take compass reading; compare to line bearing sighted from an end. Every 5 deg of bias = ~1/8 of the line length gained at the upwind end; 10 deg = ~1/4.
starts.say: Line's 10 degrees boat-favored — that's a quarter of the line, worth fighting for.

starts.rule: Start at the end that matches the side you want
starts.detail: Pick the end that leads to your preferred side of the first beat; big bias or long line can override.
starts.say: We want the right, and the boat end is favored — easy call, start up there.

starts.detail: A coming shift, pressure or current can make the downwind end better; boat-end starters reach a right shift first. A 10 deg boat-end bias needs >10 deg of expected left shift (or clear current/pressure on the left) to justify the pin.
starts.say: Pin is slightly down but the breeze is better left — the bias isn't big enough to fight it.
No clear side yet — start middle with clear air and keep options.

starts.rule: Ping the line and use time-distance
starts.detail: Use app GPS pings at both ends to compute line bias and distance-to-line; combine with boat speed for time-to-burn.
starts.say: You're 40 seconds from the line at this speed with 55 to go — burn 15.
starts.note: Ping method is standard practice; time-distance not covered in retrieved source.

starts.detail: Current pushing upwind sets the fleet over early (OCS risk); current with the wind makes the fleet sag. Right-to-left current opens a hole at the boat end and jams the pin; left-to-right causes barging at the boat and an easier pin.
starts.say: Ebb is pushing us toward the line — hang back a length further than feels right.

starts.rule: Light air + strong current = patience and position
starts.detail: Annapolis NOOD days with light southerly and strong current produced multiple general recalls and OCS boats.
starts.say: Light air and strong current — expect a recall; don't be the boat over early.

upwind.detail: Works in any condition if you can predict the next shift: in oscillating = tack on headers; in persistent = go to the favored side.
upwind.say: Next shift is likely right, so keep heading that way.

upwind.detail: Lifts make you overstand; headers let leeward boats cross. Sail the longer tack first when unsure — it's more likely the lifted one and keeps you central.
upwind.say: We're near the layline with half a beat left — tack back toward the middle.

upwind.rule: Leverage: only take it when you have a reason
upwind.detail: Separation from the fleet multiplies gains and losses from shifts; consolidate (cross and get back in front of the group) when a shift puts you ahead.
upwind.say: That lift put us up — cross them now and lock it in.
upwind.note: Leverage term from North U; consolidation rule from Dellenbaugh 'cross em when you can'.

upwind.rule: Covering: tight vs loose vs none
upwind.detail: Tight cover (bad air on them) to force a tack, e.g. near layline or to pull a lone boat back; loose cover (between them and the mark, not in their air) to keep a group behind; no cover when you're going to the favored side and they head into less wind/worse current.
upwind.say: Loose cover — stay between them and the mark without fouling their air.

upwind.rule: Current: more in deep water, less in shallows
upwind.detail: In adverse current, the shallower side often wins; current turns first in shallow water.
upwind.say: Ebb's against us — work the shallower left where the current is weaker.

upwind.rule: Head first to the side where current helps
upwind.detail: With cross-current, sail into it first to stay centered and avoid being swept to a corner.
upwind.say: Current's setting us right — sail the tack that fights it first.

upwind.detail: Annapolis NW + ebb example: right had more wind and more adverse current; left had less of both plus bigger shifts near Spa Creek. Watch the water and go where the puffs are consistent.
upwind.say: Right has more breeze but more ebb — I see steady puffs on the left, so left it is.

upwind.detail: Chesapeake chop is short and steep (shallow water, long fetch, powerboat wake on sunny weekends): keep the boat powered up, foot slightly, don't pinch.
upwind.say: Short steep chop — foot off a couple degrees and keep it powered.

downwind.rule: Gybe on the lifts (stay on the headed gybe)
downwind.detail: Downwind in oscillating breeze, a lift means gybe; stay on the headed gybe — it points you closer to the mark. Stay away from downwind laylines.
downwind.say: We just got lifted — gybe, the other gybe is now pointing at the mark.

downwind.detail: On the first gybe sail away from the persistent shift so both gybes are relatively headed, unless the shifted side also has more pressure — then go straight to the pressure.
downwind.say: Wind's moving right for good — gybe away from it first, but if the breeze is stronger over there, just go get it.

downwind.detail: Sail toward puffs and stay in them; bear off with the puff, head up in lulls. Assign someone to look behind for pressure.
downwind.say: Puff coming from behind on port — get into it and ride it down.

downwind.detail: Use the boat's polar for target TWA/boat speed; deeper in breeze, hotter in light air. Don't over-soak in light air.
downwind.say: You're 10 degrees below target in light air — heat it up for speed.
downwind.note: Angle values must come from the boat's polar; not from source.

downwind.detail: Stay on the sides and attack when the rival gybes back to the middle; gybe on their air from 2-3 lengths, not closer than ~1 (invites a luff). Cross ahead and gybe to control the path to the mark.
downwind.say: They're gybing to the middle — gybe now and put our shadow on them.

downwind.rule: Reaches: high arc vs low arc
downwind.detail: Sail high and fast early in building breeze or a persistent header; low early in a dying breeze or a persistent lift. Head low in puffs, high in lulls.
downwind.say: Breeze is dying — get low now while there's pressure, then come up at the end.

markRoundings.detail: Approach high so you can bear away and carry speed into and out of the turn; in chop bear away after each wave.
markRoundings.say: Come in a touch high so we keep speed through the rounding.

markRoundings.rule: Approach leeward mark low, exit high and tight
markRoundings.detail: Sail low on approach and come up from below to gain speed at the mark.
markRoundings.say: Dip below the line now so we can come up hot at the mark.

markRoundings.rule: Allow for set on the layline
markRoundings.detail: Walker: 1 kt of flood pushed his boat ~600 ft to leeward over a 5-min layline leg. Overstand by the expected set, and be conservative — arrive with speed rather than squeaking.
markRoundings.say: Current will set us about 600 feet in 5 minutes — sail past the layline before tacking.

markRoundings.detail: Current running upwind (against wind) or left-to-right moves the starboard layline downwind; current with the wind or right-to-left moves it upwind.
markRoundings.say: Ebb is pushing us up — tack a bit early; the layline is lower than it looks.

markRoundings.rule: In light air and strong current, watch flow at the mark
markRoundings.detail: Annapolis spring: pay close attention to current direction at roundings in light air.
markRoundings.say: Current is sweeping onto the mark — give it a boat length extra.

markRoundings.rule: Exit: line up a transit for the next leg
markRoundings.detail: After rounding, line up a land feature behind the next mark to see set; aim above or below to compensate.
markRoundings.say: Line the mark up with the water tower — if it drifts, we're being set.

current.detail: When possible, choose the tack where current hits the leeward bow so it pushes you upwind toward the mark.
current.say: On starboard the ebb is on our lee bow — this is the tack to be on.
current.note: Lee-bow principle is standard; retrieved source covers favorable-side rule, not the term itself.

current.rule: In adverse current, hug the shallows (if safe)
current.detail: Current is weaker in shallow water; respect depth and channel markers (locals sail close to Horn Point shoal with board down, but respect channel markers).
current.say: Ebb's against us — get into the shallower water, but watch the depth.

current.rule: In favorable current, go to deep water
current.detail: Channel has the strongest flow; current rips appear in deeper channel water.
current.say: Flood is with us — get out in the channel where it runs hardest.

current.detail: When the current changes, shallow areas change first, so the course can have mixed currents near the change.
current.say: Slack is due — the shore side will turn fair before the channel does.

current.rule: Read the water, don't trust tables blindly
current.detail: Watch crab-pot floats, committee boat, pin, anchored ships (can lie stern-to-wind in strong current/light wind), current lines and foam. Tables are off with river flow and recent rain.
current.say: Crab pots are leaning north — that's flood, whatever the table says.

current.detail: When wind opposes current waves steepen and the layline moves downwind; prepare for extra tacks.
current.say: Wind against the ebb — chop will stack up; expect to need an extra tack.

chesapeake.pattern: Prevailing south / southwest (summer default, Bermuda High)
chesapeake.wind: Breeze usually 160-220 deg straight up the bay; thermals can add ~5 kt to 10-12 kt (Pline). NWS often forecasts 'southerly channeling' up the Bay pushing toward SCA levels. Late spring/summer can be light and fickle with local effects.
chesapeake.waves: Long fetch down the bay plus shallow water = short, steep chop that builds over the afternoon; worse on sunny weekends with powerboat wake.
chesapeake.handling: Keep the boat powered up; foot for speed; set up for chop.
chesapeake.strategy: Local rule: wind from the south, go right. Annapolis Neck shadows SW breeze near shore (smaller chop, less pressure).
chesapeake.say: Classic southerly up the bay — right side usually pays here, and keep her powered through the chop.

chesapeake.wind: Day before a cold front: backs SW, W, NW, then tends to shift right as the front approaches; can reach ~20 kt, moderately shifty.
chesapeake.waves: Smaller chop when Annapolis Neck shadows the course.
chesapeake.strategy: Play the clocking trend; westerlies are unstable with 25+ deg shifts and heavy puffs — extra breeze off the Severn and the nearest weather shore.
chesapeake.say: Westerly ahead of the front — big shifts and heavy puffs; tack on the shifts and watch the Severn for pressure.

chesapeake.wind: NW runs down the Severn ~1 day after a front; 20-60 deg shifts, big pressure differences, strong left puffs often lasting ~10 min. Can blow ~20 kt for a few days then clock NE and fade. Northerlies crossing land: steady pressure but fast, very large shifts. Gusts near 30 kt possible over the open channel in strong NW.
chesapeake.waves: Short steep chop down the bay; strong NW also tends to produce a strong, long ebb (with the wind) — wind-over-ebb is milder, but NW against flood or at the Potomac mouth steepens seas.
chesapeake.handling: Depower for puffs; crew weight out; expect cold.
chesapeake.strategy: Local rule: wind from the north, go left. Don't count on a left puff lasting a full beat. As high pressure builds puffs thin and holes deepen; afternoon heating can kill it early. Strong ebb in NW: start high and compensate at each windward mark.
chesapeake.say: Post-frontal northwester — left usually pays, but these puffs last about ten minutes, so take them and consolidate.

chesapeake.pattern: Easterly / northeast (low pressure, often light and dying)
chesapeake.wind: Cool rainy easterly under 10 kt with pressure differences across the course; often the dying end of a northerly. NE in river/harbor is the shiftiest, random not rhythmic; steadier out in the Bay.
chesapeake.waves: Typically small locally; strong NE/SE storms bring the biggest waves into Annapolis harbor.
chesapeake.strategy: Far right (new wind) or far left (old pressure); middle suffers.
chesapeake.say: Dying easterly — pick a corner and commit; the middle gets nothing.

chesapeake.wind: Weak at Annapolis; fills earlier with a SE background veering SW, little/none with W or NW background. Fills at Sandy Point more often than Kent Island -> big cross-bay shifts. Can fight a dying northerly creating a half-mile neutral zone. Cumulus along the shoreline signals it.
chesapeake.waves: Steady light wind but often heavy powerboat chop.
chesapeake.handling: Keep moving through chop; don't pinch.
chesapeake.strategy: Left shifts often pay before it fully fills; once established it veers — then favor right.
chesapeake.say: Cumulus over the western shore — the bay breeze is coming; expect lefts first, then a veer right.

chesapeake.pattern: Thunderstorms / squalls (May-Sept, along fronts and summer afternoons)
chesapeake.wind: Gusty, erratic outflow; frontal storms' shifts are somewhat more predictable than purely thermal ones. May is the wettest month. Wave models underpredict waves in localized storms.
chesapeake.handling: Reef/douse early; check NWS Special Marine Warnings; head for safety.
chesapeake.strategy: Safety overrides tactics. Before arrival, outflow can bring a big shift toward the storm cell's direction.
chesapeake.say: Cell building to the west — get the kite down now; racing comes second.

chesapeake.pattern: Wind against current at Thomas Point / Bay Bridge
chesapeake.wind: Bay Bridge is the narrowest part of the bay with the highest current speeds near Annapolis.
chesapeake.waves: Wind opposing current steepens chop markedly (best documented by Coast Pilot for the Potomac mouth in NW vs ebb; same physics applies at Thomas Point and the bridge).
chesapeake.handling: Expect slamming; foot and power through.
chesapeake.strategy: Expect the layline to move downwind in adverse current; in light air near the Bridge, current dominates — get out of it or use it.
chesapeake.say: Southerly against the ebb off Thomas Point — chop will be nasty here; power up and expect the layline to sag.

chesapeake.pattern: Typical current strength and timing near Annapolis
facts: Tidal range ~2 ft, semidiurnal (two highs/two lows); 3-4 ft on moon tides. [expert, Pline]
Main-bay current typically ~1 kt or less off Annapolis; Bay Bridge narrows carry the strongest current. [expert]
Thomas Point example: ebb a little over 1 kt; slack came more than 3 h after low water. [measured-anecdotal, Chesapeake Bay Magazine]
Current turns a few hours AFTER high/low water, not at it — slack roughly 3 h after LW/HW; CBOFS plots near Poplar Island show max flood ~1.5 h after high tide. [measured-anecdotal]
Tide crest travels up the bay ~15 mph. [measured]
Severn River current seldom exceeds 0.5 kt; Magothy entrance ~0.6 kt flood / 0.3 kt ebb. [measured, NOAA Coast Pilot 3 ch.13]
Ebb runs N->S, flood S->N. Ebbs often stronger/longer than floods in spring due to river runoff; after heavy rain expect ebb. [expert]

Strong northerly delays high tide and lengthens/strengthens the ebb; very strong northerly may mean no high tide; post-nor'easter drain can produce 18+ h of continuous ebb. Strong N or S weakens tidal flow. [expert/measured-anecdotal]
Eddy near Greenbury Point can run opposite the main bay current. Foam line SE from the Naval Academy breakwater marks a current shear (stronger on its east side). [lore/expert]
Wind strongly influences Severn tides. [measured, Coast Pilot]
chesapeake.say: Low water was at noon, so expect the flood to start around three — the shallows will turn first.

chesapeake.wind: Summer evenings: often southerly/southeasterly up the Bay; nights abandoned for thunderstorms are common; light-air nights in July-August. Evening thermal decay can leave holes near the finish.
chesapeake.waves: Waves roll up the Bay in a solid southerly — good surfing downwind; weekday powerboat wake lighter than weekends.
chesapeake.handling: Big crowded fleet; keep clear air, conservative at crowded marks.
chesapeake.strategy: Big fleets and short courses magnify starts and mark roundings; watch for storms building to the west; in a dying evening breeze sail toward remaining pressure.
chesapeake.say: Crowded Wednesday-night start — clean air beats a perfect end; and keep an eye on that cell to the west.

chesapeake.wind: April: stronger, NW and NE dominated (SE also common/strong from stalled fronts). May: weaker, more southerly/variable, wettest month. Early May average ~7 kt from W. July-August often light and hot. Spring and fall are best; fall NW post-frontal blows are the big-breeze days.
chesapeake.waves: Spring water is cold (~51F in early spring) relative to air, suppressing sea breeze.
chesapeake.strategy: Identify the synoptic system first — it predicts the day.
chesapeake.say: Cold water, warm sunny air — don't wait on a sea breeze today; it probably won't come.

facts: Area A: ~1 mi east of Greenbury Point radio towers (big regattas).
Harbor is ~3x wider than the river; SE seawall reflected waves — stay clear.
Left side in SE harbor courses gets more current because it aligns with the river.
chesapeake.say: Left-side breeze here heads toward the Greenbury towers — use them as your reference.

coachPrinciples: Say it once, with the reason ('tack — 8 degree header past median').
Lead with the decision, then the why, then the confidence level.
Distinguish lore from measurement out loud when it matters ('local rule of thumb says right; current data agrees').
Update the plan when the water disagrees with the forecast or tide table — observations beat predictions.
Safety first: thunderstorms, depth near shoals, and channel traffic override any tactic.
Be quiet during maneuvers and starts' final 30 seconds except for time/distance calls.
Prefer simple, repeatable rules (sail toward the next shift; pressure first downwind) over clever ones.
Near marks, be conservative in current — arrive with speed.
Never stack more than one new instruction per call.
After the race, debrief: what shift type it was, which side paid, and whether the call matched.
